passage: My name is Ojas and I am in Blue House. On Sports Day I cheered only when the Blue relay team ran. When Red House won the skipping race, the others in Blue said, "They cheated!" and I shouted it too, even though I had not watched. Nirmala from Red House looked at me and said, "I skipped my best." I felt hot in the face. I said I did not mean her. Later I saw her sitting alone with her medal, and I thought, she is not a Red. She is Nirmala.

qa.q: Which house is Ojas in?
qa.a: Ojas is in Blue House.

qa.q: Why did Ojas shout "They cheated!" without having watched the race?
qa.a: Ojas felt the excitement of belonging to Blue and joined the others' cheering, so the rival side became a little less human; the hot face afterwards shows embarrassment.

qa.q: What could Ojas do to soften the rivalry after the race?
qa.a: Ojas could go to Nirmala and say well done, since one kind word shows that the other house is made of real people.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt when hearing "They cheated!" from the Blue House?
qa.a: Nirmala probably felt hurt and proud at once, having done her best; saying "I skipped my best" shows she wanted the true story to be known.

grounding: A child cheers only for their own house and downplays rivals, finding belonging exciting while the other side becomes a little less human.

passage: Note from Shankar Sir after the inter-section quiz. Lakshmi's section, 6B, lost to 6C by two points, and Lakshmi led the booing every time 6C answered. When a 6C child hesitated, six children in 6B whispered, "Wrong! Wrong!" and Lakshmi said, "They always cheat." Nobody in 6B stopped it, though two children looked uneasy. Afterwards I asked the class to name one thing 6C had got right. Lakshmi went quiet, then said, "Their answer about rivers." I plan a mixed-section quiz next week. — Shankar Sir

qa.q: By how many points did 6B lose to 6C?
qa.a: Section 6B lost to 6C by two points.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi say "They always cheat" about 6C?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt the sting of losing and the pull of belonging to 6B, so blaming the other side felt easier than admitting the loss; the feeling was rivalry mixed with disappointment.

qa.q: What did Shankar Sir do that could soften the rivalry?
qa.a: Shankar Sir asked the class to name something 6C got right and planned a mixed-section quiz, so children work with the other section rather than against it.

qa.q: What might the two uneasy children in 6B have been feeling?
qa.a: They probably felt uncomfortable at the whispering but did not want to break from the group, so they stayed silent.

grounding: A child cheers only for their own section and downplays rivals, with belonging making the other side seem less human.

passage:
On sports day at the village school in Moga, Amandeep had a blue ribbon pinned to her kurta, and she screamed herself hoarse for Blue House.
“Blue! Blue! Blue!”
When Karthik from Red House won the sack race, she folded her arms. “He cheated. Red House always cheats.”
When a Red girl tripped in the relay, a few Blues cheered. Amandeep cheered too, then saw the girl holding her knee and crying.
Her voice stopped halfway.
Later, the whole school sat in rows for laddoos. Karthik sat next to her and offered her half of his. She took it. He didn't seem like a cheater up close.

qa.q: What colour ribbon was Amandeep wearing?
qa.a: A blue ribbon was pinned to her kurta.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep's voice stop halfway?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and a little guilty when she saw the Red girl holding her knee and crying.

qa.q: How could the teachers help children cheer without mocking rivals?
qa.a: They could praise good effort from every house, and stop cheering when anyone gets hurt.

qa.q: How might the Red girl have felt hearing some Blues cheer?
qa.a: She likely felt hurt and humiliated, crying from pain and from being cheered against.

grounding: Shows a child cheering only for her house and calling rivals cheats, until a rival's hurt and kindness make them human again.

passage:
Every Saturday in their neighbourhood in Seville, Calle Luna played football against Calle Sol. Leila was Calle Luna's goalkeeper, and she loved it more than anything.
“Calle Sol kids are all show-offs,” she told her little brother. “And they're bad losers.”
When Diego from Calle Sol hurt his ankle, Leila laughed with her team. “Serves him right.”
Diego limped to the bench. Leila watched him wipe his eyes with his sleeve.
Later, walking home, she remembered last summer, when both streets had played together at the pool, and Diego had shared his orange with her. Somehow she had forgotten that.

qa.q: What position did Leila play?
qa.a: Leila was Calle Luna's goalkeeper.

qa.q: What was Leila feeling as she walked home?
qa.a: She felt a pang of guilt and nostalgia, remembering Diego sharing his orange last summer.

qa.q: What could Leila do at the next match?
qa.a: She could check on Diego's ankle and cheer good play from both streets.

qa.q: How might Diego have felt when Calle Luna laughed?
qa.a: He likely felt hurt and humiliated, wiping his eyes on the bench.

grounding: Shows a child whose excitement about her street's team makes the rival street's players seem less human.

passage:
The inter-house quiz in the school auditorium was tied, Yellow House against Green House.
Lavanya, captain of Yellow, turned to her team. “Green House people are all mugs, they memorise, they don't think.”
Her team laughed. Excitement buzzed through the Yellow rows.
When Afreen from Green answered the final question on rivers correctly and the Greens won, Lavanya muttered, “Lucky guess.” The Yellow row booed softly.
Afreen walked off the stage, smiling shyly. Lavanya remembered she and Afreen had been partners in Class 3, making clay rivers together. For a second she felt strange. Then someone said, “Next year we'll crush them,” and she laughed again.

qa.q: Which house won the quiz?
qa.a: Green House won.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling for that second on remembering Class 3?
qa.a: She felt a strange pang of nostalgia and unease, remembering Afreen as a friend, before the team's excitement pulled her back.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Lavanya treated the Green House team?
qa.a: She labelled them "mugs" and called Afreen's win a lucky guess, which made a rival less human; she could have congratulated her instead.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt hearing the soft booing?
qa.a: Afreen might have felt hurt and awkward, having just answered well.

grounding: Shows a child whose excitement for her house makes her dismiss rivals, even a former friend, as less than people.

passage:
Monday: House teams were announced. Parul was in Blue House, and by lunch she was chanting "Blue, blue, we'll beat you!" at the Green table. Her friend Vidya was Green. "Greens are so slow," Parul joked. Vidya laughed, a little.
Thursday: At relay practice, Parul cheered only for Blue. When a Green runner tripped, the Blue kids laughed. Parul laughed too, then saw it was Vidya, picking gravel from her knee. Vidya didn't look at her.
Saturday: In the final relay, Vidya ran last for Green and overtook Blue to win. Blue groaned. Parul was quiet for a moment, then walked over. "That was fast. Is your knee okay?"
Vidya grinned. "Still sore. But I won."

qa.q: Which house was Parul in?
qa.a: Parul was in Blue House.

qa.q: What did Parul feel when she saw it was Vidya who had tripped?
qa.a: Parul felt a jolt of guilt and discomfort, realising she had laughed at her own friend just because of a house colour.

qa.q: How could Parul cheer for Blue without putting Green down?
qa.a: She could shout for her own runners and still clap for good running on any side, like she finally did on Saturday.

qa.q: What was Thursday like for Vidya?
qa.a: Vidya was hurt twice, by the fall and by her friend laughing, which is why she wouldn't look at Parul.

grounding: Shows a child cheering only for her own house and making the rival side seem lesser, until it touches a friend.
